frames.narration: A user saved a file. The part of Dropbox that handles files has split it into blocks of up to 4 MB, compressed and encrypted each one, and named it by its hash. It sends one block to a Frontend of Magic Pocket.

The Frontend first asks the Block Index whether this hash is already stored. The Block Index is a sharded MySQL database that maps each block to the cell and bucket that hold it. Here the answer is no.

The Frontend already knows, from asking each cell, which volumes are open for new writes. It picks one in a way that spreads load and keeps traffic inside a cluster, then asks the Replication Table which storage nodes hold that volume.

messages.label: which nodes hold this open volume?

frames.narration: The Frontend sends the block to every storage node of the volume. Each one writes it to disk and flushes it (fsync) before it answers. If any of them fails, the Frontend retries with another volume, possibly in another cell.
Only now does the Frontend add the Block Index entry (hash to cell, bucket and checksum) and tell the caller the block is stored. If a write fails part way, the Master later cleans up the leftovers.

Later the volume is full and closed, so it never changes again. Closed volumes can be moved safely, so the Master asks a Volume Manager to re-encode the buckets of closed volumes from copies into an erasure coded form that needs less disk.

A read goes the other way. The Frontend looks up the cell and bucket in the Block Index, the volume and nodes in the Replication Table, and fetches the block from one storage node. Dropbox encodes so that a whole block can be read from a single node.

Now a storage node stays offline. If it is still gone after 15 minutes the Master closes its volumes and plans a repair that copies from many other nodes at once. The new layout counts only when the Master raises the volume's generation number and records the new nodes in the Replication Table.
